How does `bindings` read a file at `manifest_revision`: from a Git object, from a checked-out directory that must match the revision, or through another revision-addressed manifest provider, and what failure is returned when the revision cannot be resolved?

precedent.topic: Mechanism for reading repository files at a manifest revision
quotes:
**The manifest at a revision**: `manifest_location` is a directory inside a
git repository and `manifest_revision` a commit of it; `bindings` reads
`<service_id>.json` of that directory at that commit as a git object, never
from the working tree, so a record changes only with the configured revision
(A08 rules 1 and 6).
precedent.why: The later contract fixes both revision semantics and immutable access through Git objects rather than the working tree.

check_installed_instances: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Takes the services the installation holds a credential for, in service_id order by Unicode code point, and for each raises RefusedError naming that service at the first failure: first the credential header name equals a name in the imported KERNEL_SET_HEADER_NAMES constant compared without regard to case, host included, checked without reading the manifest; then, only when the installation selects an instance for the service, its record read by read_service_record fails any check, or the selected instance named in the record has a required header whose name equals the credential header name compared without regard to case.

   `https` URL with a host counts as none — or names one required header
   twice, or names one the kernel sets itself (`host`, `accept-encoding`,
   `content-type`, `content-length`, A10 rule 7) other than `host`, which an

topics.topic: Duplicate-preserving input representation for canonical_bytes
questions: Does `canonical_bytes` receive raw JSON text or a parsed representation that preserves duplicate-member detection, since an ordinary parsed JSON value has already lost duplicate keys?
What representation reaches `canonical_bytes` so that it can detect duplicate object keys after JSON parsing?

judgement.why: The same duplicate-preserving canonical input question was already judged, and the quoted text was not changed.

quotes:
`canonical_bytes` parses JSON text, refuses a duplicate member name,
   a non-finite number and an integer outside ±(2^53 − 1), which an IEEE double
   cannot hold exactly, and emits the JCS form.

canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.

canonical_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise NonCanonicalValueError, with a reason naming the first offending item in text order, when json_text is not one well-formed JSON value, when an object repeats a member name at any depth, when it holds a non-finite number (NaN, Infinity or -Infinity tokens, which the default Python parser would accept and therefore MUST be rejected explicitly), when a number written without a fraction or exponent lies outside plus or minus (2 to the power 53 minus 1), which an IEEE double cannot hold exactly, or when a string holds a lone surrogate.
precedent.why: State 6 makes canonical_bytes consume JSON text and detect repeated member names while parsing it.

topics.topic: Encoding or rejection of multipart port names and filenames
questions: How are quotes, backslashes, non-ASCII characters and control characters in port names encoded or rejected in multipart header parameters?
How are arbitrary port names encoded or escaped in multipart header parameters, and which names are refused because they cannot safely be represented?

quotes: - `name`: unique within its owner and direction;

Each part has exactly two
   headers: `Content-Disposition: form-data; name="<port>"`, with
   `filename="<port>"` added for a file part, and `Content-Type`, the port's
   media type for a file part and `application/json` for a value part, without
   parameters; nothing else.

prepare_request: [BEHAVIOR] For POST, PUT and PATCH without a file input the inputs not used in the path form one JSON object keyed by port name, sent as its RFC 8785 canonical bytes with content type application/json; with a file input the body is multipart/form-data with one part per input not used in the path in port name order, one part per file in list order for a many file port, each part having exactly the two headers Content-Disposition form-data with name set to the port, plus filename set to the port for a file part, and Content-Type, the port's media type for a file part and application/json without parameters for a value part whose content is the canonical JSON bytes.
judgement.divergence: One implementation rejects port names containing quotes, backslashes, controls or non-ASCII characters; another escapes or extended-encodes them in multipart parameters, which the proposing caller notices as refusal versus acceptance and the external service notices in the received part names and filenames.
judgement.why: Port names are only constrained to be unique while the multipart text requires them in quoted header parameters without defining their allowed character set or encoding.

For a `multipart/form-data` body, the boundary between its parts and the
    `content-length` it changes are the kernel's framing, not a difference:
    the parts themselves — name, filename, media type and content — are what
    the owner was shown and what must not differ (A10 rule 7; owner,
    2026-10-06, raised by State 2 round 80).

The body is described as the JSON body's bytes, or for
   `multipart/form-data` as the parts in order, each as its name, filename when
   present, media type and the SHA-256 of its content — the boundary, and the
   `content-length` it changes, are the kernel's framing of the parts the
   owner was shown, not a difference State 0 asks again for — so the boundary is not
   part of it: equal parts give equal descriptions.

judgement.divergence: One implementation chooses a boundary and checks that it cannot collide with any part content using one valid CRLF serialization; another uses an unchecked or differently serialized boundary, which the external service notices as a valid multipart request versus ambiguous or malformed parts.

judgement.why: The same authored trial-map completeness question was already judged, and the quoted text was not changed.

precedent.topic: Required input and expected-output port coverage in authored trial cases
quotes: add_trial_case: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Raises UnknownReferenceError for an unknown contract version; then RefusedError naming the first name in inputs that is not an input port of the contract version, then the first name in expected_outputs that is not an output port, each taken by name; then checks each input port and, when expected_outputs is given, each output port, in port name order, by fit_port_value with the imported RELEASE_CEILING_STORED_VALUE_BYTES_MAX constant for value ports and the imported RELEASE_CEILING_TRIAL_FIXTURE_BYTES_MAX constant for file ports, a file candidate taking the payload's digest, size and the port's media type; the first failing check, presence, carriage, schema then size, raises RefusedError naming port and check, and nothing is written. A trial case therefore names exactly the contract's input ports, and expected_outputs is either absent or names exactly every output port: a partial expected_outputs, and an empty object, is given and fails presence at its first missing port; only absence means no expected outputs.
precedent.why: The later notes explicitly require exact input coverage and make expected outputs either absent or complete.

Lists
   whose order carries no meaning are sorted before hashing — ports by
   (`direction`, `name`), nodes by `node_id`, edges in the edge order of A05,
   constants by (`to_node`, `to_port`) — so the same content in another order has
   the same identity; list values themselves keep their order.

2. All orders compare identifiers as strings by Unicode code point. A flow input
   or flow output endpoint has the empty string as its node, so it orders before
   every node. Within one item, the conditions are checked in the order the phase
   lists them, and the first that fails is the reason. A check that fails at
   several items names the first of them in that check's own order; a check
   whose items have no order of their own names the smallest identifier by
   code point — for cycles (phase 7) the smallest `node_id` on any cycle, for
   reach (phase 9) the smallest `node_id` of a function node none of whose
   outputs reaches, for repeated names at composition (rule 7) the smallest
   repeated name.

content_identity: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Before hashing, lists whose order carries no meaning MUST be sorted so that the same content in another order has the same identity: ports by (direction, name), flow nodes by node_id, flow edges by (to_node, to_port, from_node, from_port), flow constants by (to_node, to_port), all compared as text by Unicode code point; every other list keeps its order, in particular trial_case_ids of a corpus (corpus order is meaningful) and the elements of any JSON value.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] A content record is written with its order-free lists in the order content_identity sorts them before hashing — ports by (direction, name), flow nodes by node_id, flow edges by (to_node, to_port, from_node, from_port), flow constants by (to_node, to_port) — never in the order a caller submitted them, so equal content submitted in another order is the same record with the same lists, and every read returns those lists in that order; every other list, and every JSON value, keeps its order.
judgement.divergence: Two implementations can use different secondary ordering for edges sharing all four endpoint keys or constants sharing a target, producing different canonical list order and therefore different flow_version_id values and potentially selecting different first failing guarded edges; the composing agent notices the identity or proof-result difference.
judgement.why: The texts require order-independent hashing and deterministic first failures but give sorting keys that can tie without specifying a tie-breaker.
